picks.style: ancient greek chorus, lyre, aulos, layered female voices, sea-swaying, mournful, drifting
picks.why: The captive women's ode to the sea-breeze — where will you carry me? — running through Phthia, Delos and Athena's saffron robe. Pure lyric, no dialogue.

picks.style: tragic chorus, frame drum, aulos, low female voices, slow, ashen, building
picks.why: The night Troy fell, told from inside the bridal chamber with the spear still hanging on its peg.

picks.style: tragic duet, lyre and aulos, young female voice answered by an older one, very slow, tender, breaking
picks.why: Polyxena's farewell — one last look at the sun, one last touch of her mother's cheek — answered line for line by Hecuba.

picks.style: attic pastoral ode, aulos and lyre, warm male voice, unhurried, sunlit, nostalgic
picks.why: The old education: running under the sacred olives, crowned with white reeds, when the plane-tree whispers to the elm. The loveliest thing Aristophanes wrote.

picks.style: comic parabasis, aulos, hand drums, brash mixed chorus, striding, mock-solemn then jeering
picks.why: A real hymn — Zeus, the trident-master, Aether, the sun — turning into the Clouds' complaint that the Moon left her path and the Sun drew in his wick over Cleon.

picks.style: greek comic hymn, double aulos, tambourine, bright chorus, festive, quick, satirical
picks.why: The Clouds as goddesses of thought, argument, humbug, circumlocution and the ability to hoax — a joke shaped exactly like a hymn.

picks.style: english baroque ascent aria, chamber organ, strings, soaring soprano, rising, ecstatic
picks.why: Mount, mount, my soul on high — short driving lines climbing out of the world into the sacred magazine of light.

picks.style: declamatory georgian air, harpsichord and viols, fierce female voice, forceful, mid-tempo, indignant
picks.why: The opening of The Female Advocate, answering a satire against women by accusing it of blasphemy. The poem she is remembered for.

picks.style: english lute song, solo lute, soft female voice, hushed, gentle, unhurried
picks.why: Short-lined and secretive — love hidden in a silvan shade where only an echo will repeat it.

picks.style: english folk ballad, acoustic guitar, low strings, plain female voice, slow, plain, refrain-led
picks.why: Every stanza closes on Simplicity — an actual built-in refrain — carrying a whole village story of two lovers and one bell.

picks.style: georgian ode, flute and harpsichord, light tenor, flowing, riverine, wistful
picks.why: The Eden's poplar trembling when the poet sighs, and the naiads burnishing their green locks in the sun.

picks.style: pastoral ballad, harp and viol, gentle alto, moderate, moralising, sweet
picks.why: The myrtle's answer to the vain tulip — the violet will scent the air when you are in your dusty bed. Clean ballad quatrains.

picks.style: 18th-century english air, harpsichord and viol, alternating tenor and soprano, courtly, lilting, gently teasing
picks.why: Would you have me cease from loving? You must cease from being fair — a two-voice song already written as one.

picks.style: georgian duet, lute and chamber strings, two light voices, graceful, unhurried, wry
picks.why: Ends on the perfect stalemate — let us each go on for ever, I to ask, and you deny.

picks.style: comic ballad, fiddle and harpsichord, droll narrator voice, brisk, anapestic swing
picks.why: Jove's judgment closing the tale of Venus' stolen doves: they chose Chlorinda, and it is no crime to excel.

picks.style: oracular chant, low drone, frame drum, single grave voice, slow, foreboding
picks.why: A complete Sibylline oracle in verse — festal dancing, then hordes crossing the Danube and finding their end in Pannonia.

picks.style: hieratic solar litany, deep drone, sistrum and low drum, male voices in unison, slow, ceremonial, repetitive
picks.why: The obelisk speaking for the Sun to Ramestes — heavy repetition and epithet, which is exactly what makes it chantable.

picks.style: greek victory ode, lyre, aulos, male chorus, bright, triumphal, processional
picks.why: Euripides' epinician for Alcibiades — first, second and third in the chariot race, and the olive of Zeus.

picks.style: mock-epic invocation, kithara, low drum, grand male voice, stately, deadpan, tongue-in-cheek
picks.why: Three lines that are a whole poem: an invocation to the Muse, then Lucian coolly noting he saw the underworld and came home.
